opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the brain is a useful anchor, but I'd hold it a bit loosely in both directions.

The basic argument is that the brain runs on about 20 watts and learns from a lifetime of maybe a few billion seconds of experience, so a human-level learning algorithm can clearly be far more data- and compute-efficient than current systems. I think that's directionally right. It's an existence proof that much better algorithms are possible.

My reservations are a few. First, it's not obvious the brain's efficiency transfers to the kind of hardware and training setups we actually have. The brain is a very different substrate: massively parallel, slow, analog-ish, co-designed with its learning rules over evolutionary time. Some of its tricks might not map cleanly onto GPUs and gradient descent, so "the brain does X with Y compute" doesn't directly tell you what we can do with Y compute.

Second, the brain isn't really starting from scratch. Evolution did an enormous amount of search, and a lot of that is baked in as priors, architecture, and developmental programs. So when people say a human learns language from only so many words, part of the answer is that a huge pre-training run already happened over evolutionary history. How much that matters is pretty uncertain, and it cuts against reading lifetime learning as the full cost.

Third, the brain is a lower bound on what's possible in some sense, but it's not obviously near the ceiling. AI could end up much more efficient than the brain in some respects, for example it can copy weights, share learning across instances, and run faster. So I wouldn't treat the brain as the target either.

And finally, there's the question of how fast we'd actually find brain-level algorithms. The existence proof tells you it's possible, not that research will get there soon. That said, my overall view is that there's a lot of algorithmic headroom, and the brain makes me take that more seriously, especially once AI systems start meaningfully accelerating AI research themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution involved an enormous search and that the brain's priors reflect evolutionary history, but it does not raise the possibility that discovering a human-like algorithm may itself require research compute comparable to evolution's computational cost.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the human brain is one of the main pieces of evidence we have that very efficient, very capable intelligence is physically possible. But I have a bunch of reservations about leaning on it too hard as evidence about what AI systems will actually achieve, or how quickly.

The first is just that the comparison is really hard to make. When people say the brain runs on 20 watts and does something like 10^15 operations per second, those numbers are doing a lot of work and they're pretty uncertain. There's disagreement about how to count a synaptic event, whether you need to model things below the level of spikes, how much the brain is doing that's actually computation versus just biology keeping itself alive. You can get estimates that span several orders of magnitude depending on your assumptions. So it's not a clean benchmark.

The second reservation is that the brain was optimized under very different constraints than the ones we face. Evolution is optimizing for energy efficiency, for things like heat dissipation in a skull, for being built out of proteins and lipids, for developing over years from a genome that's quite small. It's not optimizing for the thing we care about, which is roughly "how much useful cognitive work can we get out of a given amount of silicon compute and a given amount of training." So even if the brain is extremely efficient along some axis, that doesn't tell you much about what the efficient frontier looks like for a totally different substrate with totally different tradeoffs. It could be that AI systems are way less efficient than the brain in energy terms and that's fine, because energy isn't the binding constraint. Or it could be that there are efficiencies available to us that evolution could never reach, because evolution is a pretty myopic optimizer.

The third thing is that the brain tells you something is possible, but it doesn't tell you how hard it is to get there. There's this move where people say, "the brain does it with this much compute, so once we have that much compute, we'll have human-level AI." And I think that's pretty weak. The brain is the output of billions of years of search over architectures, plus a lifetime of learning that's structured in a particular way. We might need way more compute than the brain uses to find a comparable algorithm via gradient descent, or we might need way less because we have advantages like being able to run things in parallel and copy weights. The existence proof doesn't pin that down.

And then relatedly, I think the brain sets a kind of anchor that can be misleading in both directions. On one side, people treat it as a ceiling, like efficiency can't get much better than the brain, and I don't see why that would be true. The brain has all these constraints that silicon doesn't share, and there's no principled reason to think evolution found the global optimum. On the other side, people treat it as a near-term target that we'll hit once we match some compute number, and the history of AI has a lot of cases where matching a hardware estimate didn't translate into matching the capability.

So where I actually land is something like: the brain is useful as a rough sanity check. It tells me that something in the vicinity of human-level general intelligence doesn't require absurd amounts of compute in principle, and that's a meaningful update against views where AGI needs something like a planet-sized computer. But for the questions I care about most, like how far current approaches can scale, how much algorithmic progress is left, and what the long-run efficiency frontier is, I think the brain gives you maybe one or two orders of magnitude of constraint and then you're mostly on your own. The empirical trends in AI systems themselves end up being a lot more informative to me than the biological analogy.

r001.rationale: It says the brain reflects billions of years of architectural search and that finding a comparable algorithm via gradient descent could take more compute, but it never says the required research compute could be comparable to evolution’s computational cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the brain is useful evidence, but you have to be careful about what you’re taking it as evidence for. It’s an existence proof that you can get human-level cognition with roughly the resources a brain uses. It’s not an existence proof that we know how to achieve that efficiency on GPUs, or that we’ll figure it out soon.

One reservation is that the hardware is very different. The brain has memory and computation closely integrated, and it has a lot of relatively slow parallel computation. So taking an estimate of synaptic operations and translating that directly into FLOP is pretty questionable. Depending on what a synapse is actually doing that matters for cognition, that translation could be quite misleading.

Another issue is learning. Humans get a lot of structure from evolution, and then they learn from a very different stream of experience than a language model does. So even if you knew the compute needed to run a human-level intelligence, that wouldn’t immediately tell you how much compute you need to train one.

And then there’s the question of how close the brain is to optimal. Evolution optimised under constraints that aren’t our constraints: biological components, energy availability, having to grow the system, and so on. That leaves room for artificial systems to be much more efficient in some respects. But evolution also had a long time to find useful tricks that we may not yet understand. So I’d use the brain as a rough anchor, with substantial uncertainty, rather than as a precise estimate of either the ultimate limit or what’s achievable in the next few years.

r001.rationale: The response notes that evolution provided useful structure and had a long time to find tricks, but does not say that discovering a human-like algorithm could require research compute comparable to evolution’s computational cost.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the brain is useful evidence, but you have to be pretty careful about what you’re using it as evidence for. It’s an existence proof that you can get human-level cognition with roughly the resources a brain uses. But translating that into a number of FLOP per second is quite uncertain. You need to decide which features of neurons matter computationally, and whether those features would be cheap or expensive to reproduce on digital hardware.

There’s also a distinction between the compute required to run an intelligence and the compute required to produce it. Humans learn over a lifetime, but evolution did a huge amount of work to give us a useful starting point. So you can’t just look at how much computation happens during childhood and conclude that this is enough to train a human-level AI from scratch.

And then the brain is operating under a different set of constraints. It has to fit inside a skull, use very little power, and be built out of biological components. Those constraints might make it much less efficient along some dimensions than an engineered system could be. But it also has advantages, like having memory and computation very close together, that our hardware doesn’t necessarily share.

So I’d treat it as a useful sanity check, rather than a precise estimate of what AI will cost or how quickly we’ll get there.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution did substantial work to provide humans a useful starting point, but it does not raise the possibility that research to discover a human-like algorithm could require compute comparable to evolution’s computational cost.
